claims.claim: LiGluN2A(V713C) co-expressed with wildtype GluN1a generates an inward current when illuminated with 380 nm light in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: When LiGluN2A(V713C) was co-expressed with wildtype (wt) GluN1a, photoisomerization of L-MAG1 to its cis configuration by illumination with 380 nm light (Figure 1a,c) generated an inward current (Figure 1d,e- violet bars) in both HEK293 cells (37.3 ± 2.2% of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate, n = 5, Figure 1d) and in primary cultured hippocampal neurons (30.8 ± 5.9% of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 6, Figure 1e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claims.claim: LiGluN2A(V713C) co-expressed with wildtype GluN1a generates a photocurrent that is 37.3 ± 2.2% of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: When LiGluN2A(V713C) was co-expressed with wildtype (wt) GluN1a, photoisomerization of L-MAG1 to its cis configuration by illumination with 380 nm light (Figure 1a,c) generated an inward current (Figure 1d,e- violet bars) in both HEK293 cells (37.3 ± 2.2% of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate, n = 5, Figure 1d) and in primary cultured hippocampal neurons (30.8 ± 5.9% of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 6, Figure 1e).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claims.claim: LiGluN2A(V713C) co-expressed with wildtype GluN1a generates a photocurrent that is 30.8 ± 5.9% of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA in primary cultured hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: When LiGluN2A(V713C) was co-expressed with wildtype (wt) GluN1a, photoisomerization of L-MAG1 to its cis configuration by illumination with 380 nm light (Figure 1a,c) generated an inward current (Figure 1d,e- violet bars) in both HEK293 cells (37.3 ± 2.2% of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate, n = 5, Figure 1d) and in primary cultured hippocampal neurons (30.8 ± 5.9% of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 6, Figure 1e).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claims.claim: The photocurrent of LiGluN2A(V713C) can be completely turned off by photoisomerization of L-MAG1 to trans by illumination at 488 nm.
claims.source: This photocurrent could then be completely turned off by photoisomerization of L-MAG1 to trans by illumination at 488 nm (Figure 1d,e- green bars).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figures 1d and 1e.

claims.claim: Opening and closing of LiGluN2A(V713C) channels can be accomplished by toggling between near-UV and green-light illumination at various frequencies and repeatedly.
claims.source: Since the isomerization of the azobenzene is fast (Figure 1f) (Reiner and Isacoff, 2014) and fully reversible, opening and closing of the channels could be accomplished by toggling between near-UV and green-light illumination, at various frequencies and repeatedly, to mimic various physiological patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,c, with a citation.

claims.claim: No inhibition of the current was observed during photo-agonism of LiGluN2A(V713C) in the presence of saturating glutamate or NMDA.
claims.source: No inhibition of the current was observed during photo-agonism in the presence of saturating glutamate or NMDA, suggesting that when MAG in its cis form competes with free glutamate in LiGluN2A, and is as good an agonist as glutamate.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and is based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: MAG in its cis form is as good an agonist as glutamate for LiGluN2A.
claims.source: No inhibition of the current was observed during photo-agonism in the presence of saturating glutamate or NMDA, suggesting that when MAG in its cis form competes with free glutamate in LiGluN2A, and is as good an agonist as glutamate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that no inhibition was observed during photo-agonism in the presence of saturating glutamate.

claims.claim: NMDA receptors containing LiGluN2A(V713C) preserve the glutamate potency (EC50) as seen in wt receptors that contain the GluN2A-wt subunit.
claims.source: Dose-response profiling of NMDA receptors containing LiGluN2A(V713C) (as well as other variants, see below) shows preservation of the glutamate potency (EC50) as seen in wt receptors that contain the GluN2A-wt subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b) (Anson et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2005; Hedegaard et al., 2012; Paoletti et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b, with citations.

claims.claim: LiGluN2A(V713C)-containing receptors have wt activation kinetics.
claims.source: Moreover, LiGluN2A(V713C)-containing receptors have wt activation kinetics, as assessed by fast MNI-glutamate uncaging that was designed to mimic the brief rise of glutamate that occurs in synapses due to vesicle release (Figure 1—figure supplement 2g).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2g.

claims.claim: MAG labeling had no effect on the health, resting membrane potential or membrane resistance of cultured hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Importantly, MAG labeling had no effect on the health, resting membrane potential or membrane resistance of cultured hippocampal neurons and yielded no photo-responses in neurons that did not express the cysteine-modified GluN2 subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c), indicating a lack of action on native glutamate receptors or other channels.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c.

claims.claim: MAG labeling yielded no photo-responses in neurons that did not express the cysteine-modified GluN2 subunit.
claims.source: Importantly, MAG labeling had no effect on the health, resting membrane potential or membrane resistance of cultured hippocampal neurons and yielded no photo-responses in neurons that did not express the cysteine-modified GluN2 subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c), indicating a lack of action on native glutamate receptors or other channels.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c.

claims.claim: Expression of the LiGluN2A subunit did not significantly change the amplitude of NMDA-induced current in hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Moreover, expression of the LiGluN2A subunit did not significantly change the amplitude of NMDA-induced current in hippocampal neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d), suggesting that it competes with native LiGluN2 subunits for assembly with the native GluN1, so that the total number of synaptic NMDA receptors is preserved, but now subject to photo-control.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claims.claim: LiGluN2A competes with native LiGluN2 subunits for assembly with the native GluN1, so that the total number of synaptic NMDA receptors is preserved.
claims.source: Moreover, expression of the LiGluN2A subunit did not significantly change the amplitude of NMDA-induced current in hippocampal neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d), suggesting that it competes with native LiGluN2 subunits for assembly with the native GluN1, so that the total number of synaptic NMDA receptors is preserved, but now subject to photo-control.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that expression of LiGluN2A did not change NMDA-induced current amplitude.

claims.claim: The speed of MAG photoswitching depends on light intensity.
claims.source: MAG photoswitching provides two advantageous properties for the remote control of NMDA receptors. First, since the speed of MAG photoswitching depends on light intensity so that switching can be achieved either with short high intensity pulses or longer low intensity pulses (Gorostiza et al., 2007; Reiner and Isacoff, 2014), it should be possible to sculpt the photocurrent to resemble NMDA receptor excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCNMDA).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the properties of MAG photoswitching and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: A 2 ms pulse of 375 nm light can be used to trigger substantial receptor activation of LiGluN2A(V713C) conjugated to L-MAG1.
claims.source: Using LiGluN2A(V713C) conjugated to L-MAG1, a 2 ms pulse of 375 nm light could be used to trigger substantial receptor activation (Figure 1f), with the fast rise kinetics comparable to those of EPSCNMDA kinetics observed for GluN2A-containing synaptic NMDA receptors (Bidoret et al., 2009; Erreger and Traynelis, 2005; Vicini et al., 2001; Yuan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1f, with citations.

claims.claim: The fast rise kinetics of LiGluN2A(V713C) photo-activation are comparable to those of EPSCNMDA kinetics observed for GluN2A-containing synaptic NMDA receptors.
claims.source: Using LiGluN2A(V713C) conjugated to L-MAG1, a 2 ms pulse of 375 nm light could be used to trigger substantial receptor activation (Figure 1f), with the fast rise kinetics comparable to those of EPSCNMDA kinetics observed for GluN2A-containing synaptic NMDA receptors (Bidoret et al., 2009; Erreger and Traynelis, 2005; Vicini et al., 2001; Yuan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data with published data and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Off-photoswitching of LiGluN2A(V713C) can be triggered over tens of milliseconds to mimic GluN2A deactivation kinetics.
claims.source: Then, off-photoswiching could be triggered over tens of milliseconds (Figure 1g), as typical of GluN2A, or more slowly (Figure 1h) to mimic the slower GluN2B deactivation kinetics (Erreger and Traynelis, 2005; Vicini et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1g, with citations.

claims.claim: Off-photoswitching of LiGluN2A(V713C) can be triggered more slowly to mimic the slower GluN2B deactivation kinetics.
claims.source: Then, off-photoswiching could be triggered over tens of milliseconds (Figure 1g), as typical of GluN2A, or more slowly (Figure 1h) to mimic the slower GluN2B deactivation kinetics (Erreger and Traynelis, 2005; Vicini et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1h, with citations.

claims.claim: MAG photoswitches are bistable.
claims.source: A second advantageous property is the bistability of MAG photoswitches (Gorostiza et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the properties of MAG photoswitches and is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: After switching with a brief 380 nm light pulse, photo-agonism is sustained in the dark for extended periods of time, until it is reversed by a brief 500 nm light pulse.
claims.source: After switching with a brief 380 nm light pulse, photo-agonism (or photo-antagonism, as described below) is sustained in the dark for extended periods of time, until it is reversed by a brief 500 nm light pulse, as illustrated in both hippocampal neurons, (Figure 1i) and HEK293 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1i and Figure 1—figure supplement 3e.

claims.claim: A cysteine was introduced at position 714 of GluN2B, corresponding to the 713 position that yielded the photo-agonism in GluN2A.
claims.source: Hence, we introduced a cysteine at position 714 of GluN2B, corresponding to the 713 position that yielded the photo-agonism in GluN2A (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and is shown in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: Conjugation of L-MAG1 to LiGluN2B(V714C) that was coexpressed with GluN1a in HEK293 cells yielded GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors which were activated by light.
claims.source: Indeed, conjugation of L-MAG1 to LiGluN2B(V714C) that was coexpressed with GluN1a in HEK293 cells yielded GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors which were activated by light (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: Photo-activation of LiGluN2B(V714C) in the presence of saturating glutamate yielded a small increase in current.
claims.source: Unlike with LiGluN2A(V713C), photo-activation of LiGluN2B(V714C) in the presence of saturating glutamate yielded a small increase in current (Figure 2b), suggesting that L-MAG1 is a more potent agonist than glutamate.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: L-MAG1 is a more potent agonist than glutamate for LiGluN2B(V714C).
claims.source: Unlike with LiGluN2A(V713C), photo-activation of LiGluN2B(V714C) in the presence of saturating glutamate yielded a small increase in current (Figure 2b), suggesting that L-MAG1 is a more potent agonist than glutamate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that photo-activation in the presence of saturating glutamate yielded a small increase in current.

claims.claim: LiGluN2B(V714C)-containing receptors displayed the same glutamate affinity and activation kinetics as wt GluN2B receptors.
claims.source: Importantly, LiGluN2B(V714C)-containing receptors displayed the same glutamate affinity and activation kinetics as wt GluN2B receptors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c, d and h), indicating that, as with LiGluN2A(V713C), the orthogonal light control is obtained over receptors that otherwise function normally.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c, d and h.

claims.claim: The LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B photocurrents were similar in amplitude and activation kinetics.
claims.source: The LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B photocurrents were similar in amplitude and activation kinetics (Figure 2d and e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), but the LiGluN2B photocurrent turned off ~3 times more slowly under identical light conditions (Figure 2c, inset and f and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), reminiscent of the slower deactivation kinetics of GluN2B- than GluN2A-containing receptors (Bidoret et al., 2009; Vicini et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2d, e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The LiGluN2B photocurrent turned off ~3 times more slowly than LiGluN2A under identical light conditions.
claims.source: The LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B photocurrents were similar in amplitude and activation kinetics (Figure 2d and e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), but the LiGluN2B photocurrent turned off ~3 times more slowly under identical light conditions (Figure 2c, inset and f and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), reminiscent of the slower deactivation kinetics of GluN2B- than GluN2A-containing receptors (Bidoret et al., 2009; Vicini et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2c, inset and f and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, with citations.

claims.claim: Widefield photoactivation at 380 nm of both LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B triggered an increase in EPSC frequency.
claims.source: Widefield photoactivation at 380 nm of both LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B triggered an increase in EPSC frequency and this was reversed—more slowly in LiGluN2B—by illumination at 510 nm (Figure 2c), suggesting that photoactivation of NMDA receptors containing either LiGluN2A or LiGluN2B triggered action potential firing in presynaptic neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: Photoactivation of NMDA receptors containing either LiGluN2A or LiGluN2B triggered action potential firing in presynaptic neurons.
claims.source: Widefield photoactivation at 380 nm of both LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B triggered an increase in EPSC frequency and this was reversed—more slowly in LiGluN2B—by illumination at 510 nm (Figure 2c), suggesting that photoactivation of NMDA receptors containing either LiGluN2A or LiGluN2B triggered action potential firing in presynaptic neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that photoactivation triggered an increase in EPSC frequency.

claims.claim: Photoactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster rise of excitation than LiGluN2B.
claims.source: Photoactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster rise of excitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, top insets, and f) and photodeactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster (~three fold) de-excitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, bottom insets, and g) than neurons expressing LiGluN2B.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, top insets, and f.

claims.claim: Photodeactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster (~three fold) de-excitation than neurons expressing LiGluN2B.
claims.source: Photoactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster rise of excitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, top insets, and f) and photodeactivation of LiGluN2A elicited a faster (~three fold) de-excitation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, bottom insets, and g) than neurons expressing LiGluN2B.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–b, bottom insets, and g.

claims.claim: The largest photo-antagonism was generated by L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit when expressed in hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: The largest photo-antagonism was generated by L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit when expressed in hippocampal neurons (56.4 ± 2.9% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 7) (Figure 3b, c and f), similar to the block observed in HEK293 cells (65.8 ± 4.3% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK cells, n = 9).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, c and f.

claims.claim: L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit produces 56.4 ± 2.9% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA in hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: The largest photo-antagonism was generated by L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit when expressed in hippocampal neurons (56.4 ± 2.9% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 7) (Figure 3b, c and f), similar to the block observed in HEK293 cells (65.8 ± 4.3% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK cells, n = 9).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, c and f.

claims.claim: L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit produces 65.8 ± 4.3% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: The largest photo-antagonism was generated by L-MAG0 anchored at G712C of the GluN2A subunit when expressed in hippocampal neurons (56.4 ± 2.9% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM NMDA, n = 7) (Figure 3b, c and f), similar to the block observed in HEK293 cells (65.8 ± 4.3% inhibition of the total current induced by 1 mM glutamate in HEK cells, n = 9).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, c and f.

claims.claim: Photo-antagonism of GluN2A by L-MAG0 at G712C is on par with the antagonism of GluN2A by NVP-AAM077 when applied at concentrations that maintain subunit selectivity.
claims.source: This photo-antagonism is on par with the antagonism of GluN2A by NVP-AAM077, when applied at concentrations that maintain subunit selectivity (Monaghan et al., 2012; Neyton and Paoletti, 2006; Paoletti and Neyton, 2007), and so, although incomplete (likely due to labeling efficiency, see below and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), would be predicted to have utility.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data with published data and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: A screen of cysteine mutants around the glycine-binding pocket of GluN1 identified a labeling site, E406C, where L-MAG0 functioned as photo-antagonist.
claims.source: Indeed, a screen of cysteine mutants around the glycine-binding pocket identified a labeling site, E406C, where L-MAG0 functioned as photo-antagonist (30.7 ± 1.7% inhibition of the total current neurons, n = 6) (Figure 3b, d and f), without affecting the glycine potency of the subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, d and f.

claims.claim: L-MAG0 at E406C of GluN1a produces 30.7 ± 1.7% inhibition of the total current in neurons.
claims.source: Indeed, a screen of cysteine mutants around the glycine-binding pocket identified a labeling site, E406C, where L-MAG0 functioned as photo-antagonist (30.7 ± 1.7% inhibition of the total current neurons, n = 6) (Figure 3b, d and f), without affecting the glycine potency of the subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3b, d and f.

claims.claim: L-MAG0 at E406C of GluN1a does not affect the glycine potency of the subunit.
claims.source: Indeed, a screen of cysteine mutants around the glycine-binding pocket identified a labeling site, E406C, where L-MAG0 functioned as photo-antagonist (30.7 ± 1.7% inhibition of the total current neurons, n = 6) (Figure 3b, d and f), without affecting the glycine potency of the subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f.

claims.claim: Co-expression of GluN1a(E406C) and GluN2A(G712C) in dissociated hippocampal neurons and incubation with L-MAG0 resulted in 73.8 ± 5.2% photo-inhibition of the total NMDA-induced current.
claims.source: When the photo-antagonizable GluN1a(E406C) and GluN2A(G712C) subunits were co-expressed in dissociated hippocampal neurons and incubated with L-MAG0, their combined effect resulted in 73.8 ± 5.2% (n = 4) photo-inhibition of the total NMDA-induced current in neurons (Figure 3e,f).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3e,f.

claims.claim: Photo-antagonism with 370 nm light hyperpolarized cells and suppressed firing in cultured hippocampal neurons transfected with GluN2A(G712C) and GluN1a(E406C) and labeled with L-MAG0.
claims.source: Cultured hippocampal neurons from wt rats (C57BL) transfected with the photo-antagonizing GluN2A(G712C) subunit in combination with photo-antagonizing GluN1a(E406C), labeled with L-MAG0 and under green light illumination, exhibited typical action potential activity under current clamp recordings. Photo-antagonism with 370 nm light hyperpolarized cells and suppressed firing (Figure 4a,b), as seen with conventional NMDA receptor blockers.
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claims.claim: No photo-effect was seen in non-transfected cells labeled with L-MAG0.
claims.source: No such photo-effect was seen in non-transfected cells (Figure 4c,d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4c,d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Reversal of photo-antagonism by 510 nm light elicited a gradual repolarization.

results.result: The authors engineered a family of four photoswitchable NMDA receptor subunits (LiGluNs) using MAG photoswitches that can be reversibly controlled with light. LiGluN2A(V713C) and LiGluN2B(V714C) were created as photo-agonists that generate inward currents when illuminated with 380 nm light and turn off with 488-510 nm light. These engineered receptors preserve wild-type glutamate potency, activation kinetics, and do not alter total NMDA receptor expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C33-C35, C41-C45, C48-C53, C61-C62, C65, and C120 collectively demonstrate successful engineering of light-gated NMDA receptor subunits. The data show reversible photocurrents in both HEK293 cells and hippocampal neurons (Figures 1d-e), preserved pharmacological properties (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and lack of toxicity or non-specific effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The quantitative measurements with error bars and sample sizes support the claims.

results.result: The temporal properties of MAG photoswitching can be controlled by light intensity to mimic physiological NMDA receptor kinetics. Brief high-intensity pulses (2 ms at 375 nm) trigger fast activation comparable to synaptic NMDA receptors, while the deactivation speed can be tuned from tens to hundreds of milliseconds. MAG photoswitches are bistable, maintaining their state in darkness until reversed by light.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 are supported by experimental data in Figures 1f-i showing controlled activation/deactivation kinetics with appropriate comparisons to published synaptic NMDA receptor kinetics (with citations). The bistability is demonstrated in Figure 1i showing sustained photocurrents in darkness. The ability to sculpt temporal profiles addresses a key advantage of the approach.

results.result: LiGluN2A and LiGluN2B photocurrents have similar amplitudes and activation kinetics, but LiGluN2B deactivates approximately 3 times more slowly than LiGluN2A under identical light conditions. Photoactivation of both subtypes triggers action potential firing in presynaptic neurons, as evidenced by increased EPSC frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are supported by comparative data in Figure 2c-g and Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2. The ~3-fold difference in deactivation kinetics is quantified and statistically significant (p<0.001, Mann-Whitney test shown in supplement). The inference about presynaptic action potentials (C69) is reasonable based on increased EPSC frequency, though direct confirmation would strengthen this claim.

results.result: Photo-antagonist LiGluN subunits were developed by attaching L-MAG0 at positions where the glutamate moiety blocks ligand binding. LiGluN2A(G712C) produces 56-66% inhibition of NMDA currents, comparable to the selective antagonist NVP-AAM077. LiGluN1a(E406C) produces 31% inhibition without affecting glycine potency. Combined expression of both photo-antagonist subunits yields 74% inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C79 are supported by quantitative data in Figure 3b-f with appropriate sample sizes and error bars. The comparison to NVP-AAM077 (C75) is supported by citations. The preservation of glycine potency (C78) is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e,f. The additive effect of combining both photo-antagonist subunits (C79) demonstrates the approach works at both binding sites.

results.result: Photo-antagonism of LiGluN2A(G712C) and LiGluN1a(E406C) with 370 nm light hyperpolarizes cultured hippocampal neurons and suppresses action potential firing, with gradual recovery upon 510 nm illumination. This effect is specific to transfected neurons, with no photo-effect in non-transfected controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by current clamp data in Figure 4a-d and voltage clamp data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. Statistical analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) shows significant effects in transfected but not non-transfected neurons. The specificity controls (C81, C84) are essential and properly demonstrated.

results.result: LiGluN subunits incorporate into synaptic NMDA receptors at autapses without significantly changing receptor number or kinetics. Photo-antagonism reversibly inhibits evoked NMDA EPSCs by 20-50%, with the degree of inhibition varying primarily with labeling efficiency rather than total receptor expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C92 are supported by autapse recordings in Figure 5. The similarity of eEPSC amplitude and kinetics between transfected and non-transfected neurons (C85) supports normal incorporation. Reversible photo-antagonism is demonstrated in Figure 5c-d. The lack of correlation between inhibition magnitude and EPSC amplitude (C90, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b) supports the labeling efficiency interpretation (C91), though this remains somewhat indirect.

results.result: Photo-antagonism of LiGluN2A and LiGluN1a blocks LTP induction in hippocampal CA1 neurons following Schaffer collateral stimulation. Slices with photo-antagonism OFF (green light) showed robust LTP (185% of baseline), while slices with photo-antagonism ON (violet light) showed no LTP (67% of baseline). Control experiments demonstrate this effect is specific to photo-antagonism and not due to the light protocol itself.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C99 are supported by LTP experiments in Figure 6 using organotypic slices from GluN2A-knockout mice. The experimental design is appropriate with proper controls including unlabeled slices exposed to 390 nm light (C96). Statistical significance is shown (p-value indicated in Figure 6d). The use of knockout mice ensures specificity for the introduced LiGluN subunits. This demonstrates functional control over a key form of synaptic plasticity.

results.result: Single-spine photo-agonism of LiGluN2A(V713C) induces spine-specific calcium elevation and structural plasticity. Illumination at 405 nm triggers calcium rises confined to the illuminated spine and induces spine expansion that peaks at ~5 minutes (167% of baseline) and persists for at least 45 minutes (131% of baseline). Non-illuminated nearby spines and unlabeled controls show no response.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C107 are supported by single-spine imaging data in Figure 7. Calcium compartmentalization is shown with R-GECO (Figure 7b-c). Spine expansion is quantified with appropriate statistics (paired t-tests, p<0.001) and proper controls (nearby spines, unlabeled slices). The conclusion that activation of postsynaptic GluN2A is sufficient for structural LTP (C107) is supported but should be interpreted cautiously as this is in a knockout background with artificial stimulation.

results.result: Photo-antagonism of LiGluN1a/GluN2A reversibly blocks glutamate uncaging-induced spine expansion at single synapses. During photo-antagonism, glutamate uncaging produces only transient expansion (118% peak, returning to baseline). After removing photo-antagonism with green light, a second uncaging bout induces persistent expansion (147% above new baseline).
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are supported by single-spine uncaging experiments in Figure 8. The experimental design cleverly uses two successive uncaging bouts to demonstrate reversibility and confirm spine competence. Statistical analysis shows the first expansion is not significant (p>0.1) while the second is significant (p<0.01). Controls of nearby spines are included (C110). This demonstrates temporal gating of structural plasticity at individual synapses.

results.result: In vivo photo-antagonism of LiGluN2A(G712C) in transgenic zebrafish disrupts activity-dependent pruning of retinal ganglion cell axons during the 5-7 dpf critical period. Episodic photo-antagonism produces a 16.4% increase in arbor radius, comparable to 25 μM MK-801 treatment (13.8% increase), without affecting initial development or general behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C119 are supported by in vivo zebrafish experiments in Figure 9. The transgenic line is properly characterized (C112-C114). The photo-antagonism effect is statistically significant and comparable to MK-801 (C115-C117), validating the approach. Behavioral controls (C118, Figure 9—figure supplement 1b) demonstrate lack of toxicity. This demonstrates the utility of the approach for chronic in vivo manipulations. The episodic illumination protocol (10 s every 30 min) cleverly exploits MAG bistability.

results.result: Background claims about NMDA receptor structure, function, and biological roles establish the scientific context and motivation for developing subunit-specific optical control tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C11-C17 are general knowledge statements about NMDA receptors supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary background but are not novel findings of this study. The complexity described (C17) motivates the need for the tools developed in this work.

results.result: Existing approaches for manipulating NMDA receptors (pharmacological agents, genetic manipulations, caged compounds, photo-reactive amino acids) have limitations in temporal control, spatial confinement, reversibility, or subunit specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C32 accurately describe limitations of existing approaches and are supported by appropriate citations. These establish the need for the new tools but are not novel findings. The characterization of limitations is fair and well-documented in the literature.

results.result: PTL technology has been previously applied to generate light-gated versions of various neurotransmitter receptors and channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 describe prior applications of PTL technology and are supported by appropriate citations. This establishes the technical foundation for the current work but represents prior art rather than novel findings.

results.result: MAG in its cis form acts as a full agonist for LiGluN2A (comparable to glutamate) but as a super-agonist for LiGluN2B (more potent than glutamate), as inferred from responses in the presence of saturating glutamate.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 and C63-C64 are inferences based on observations during saturating glutamate application (Figures 1d-e, 2b). For LiGluN2A, no additional current during photo-agonism suggests equal efficacy (C47). For LiGluN2B, a small increase suggests higher potency (C64). These are reasonable inferences but indirect measurements. Direct dose-response curves for MAG would strengthen these claims.

results.result: Summary claims about the properties and capabilities of the LiGluN toolset, including subunit selectivity, normal function, synaptic incorporation, and applications to studying NMDA receptor function.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C130 and C141 are summary statements supported by the collective experimental evidence presented throughout the paper. These synthesize the major findings but do not represent independent results. They accurately reflect what was demonstrated experimentally.

results.result: Discussion of technical limitations including incomplete labeling efficiency, partial MAG isomerization, stereochemistry effects, temporal constraints of maleimide conjugation, and receptor turnover.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C137 acknowledge limitations of the approach and are supported by citations and logical inference. The incomplete photo-agonism/antagonism (C131) is evident in the data (typically 30-75% of maximum). These are honest assessments of limitations, though some (like C133) are speculative. The discussion of SNAP-tag alternatives (C134) points to ongoing improvements.

results.result: Discussion of future directions including two-photon compatible MAG variants and potential applications in various model organisms and for studying NMDA receptor mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 and C142 discuss future possibilities supported by citations to recent advances. However, these are speculative statements about potential applications rather than demonstrated results. The citations support that two-photon MAGs exist (C138) and that the approach works in some model organisms (C140), but broader applications remain to be demonstrated.
